title: What Is Included in a New HVAC System Install?
h1: What Is Included in a New HVAC System Installation?
description: A new HVAC install includes more than the equipment. Learn what a complete job covers, from load calculation and permits to startup, testing and haul-away.
quick_answer: A complete HVAC installation usually includes a sizing calculation, the indoor and outdoor equipment, a matched coil, refrigerant lines, a thermostat, electrical and drain connections, venting for gas furnaces, permits and inspection, startup and testing, and removal of the old system. Ductwork changes, electrical panel upgrades and add-ons are often quoted separately.
body:
Two estimates for a new system can look very different, even for similar equipment. Often the difference is what's included in the job. Knowing what a complete installation covers helps you compare quotes fairly and avoid surprises later.

What happens before the installation?

A good install starts with a visit to your home, not a quote over the phone. The technician should:

  • Look at your current equipment, its location and how it's vented
  • Inspect the ductwork, especially in the attic
  • Ask about comfort problems like hot rooms, noise or dust
  • Size the new system based on the house itself, including square footage, insulation, windows and sun exposure

Sizing matters. A system that's too big short cycles and leaves humidity behind. One that's too small runs constantly on hot inland afternoons. Replacing a unit with the same size as the old one isn't always right, especially if you've added insulation, windows or rooms.

What equipment comes with a new system?

A typical split system replacement includes:

  • Heating unit. A gas furnace or an air handler for a heat pump.
  • Outdoor unit. An AC condenser or heat pump.
  • Evaporator coil. A coil matched to the outdoor unit so they work together as designed.
  • Thermostat. Usually a new thermostat compatible with the equipment.
  • Pad or stand. A level base for the outdoor unit.

Ask whether the coil is new and matched. Pairing a new outdoor unit with an old coil can hurt efficiency and reliability.

What installation work should be included?

  1. Removing the old equipment and recovering refrigerant properly.
  2. Refrigerant lines. Installing new lines or cleaning and pressure testing existing ones if they can be reused.
  3. Electrical connections to the existing circuit, including a disconnect at the outdoor unit.
  4. Condensate drain and, for attic installs, a secondary pan or safety switch to protect the ceiling.
  5. Venting for gas furnaces, sized and run to code.
  6. Connecting to the ductwork with new transitions sealed at the equipment.
  7. Vacuum and charge. Evacuating the lines and setting the refrigerant charge.
  8. Startup and testing of heating and cooling, airflow and safety controls.
  9. Cleanup and haul-away of the old equipment.

Are permits and inspections part of the job?

They should be. In California, replacing heating and cooling equipment generally requires a permit, and the work is inspected afterward. Depending on the job and location, the state energy code may also call for duct leakage testing or other verification. A permitted install protects you if questions come up when you sell the house, and it confirms the work was checked by someone other than the installer.

If a quote doesn't mention permits, ask about it directly.

What is often quoted separately?

These items may or may not be part of your job, so check the estimate:

  • Replacing or redesigning ductwork
  • Electrical panel or circuit upgrades, which can come up when switching to a heat pump
  • Adding zoning, a media filter, a UV light or a dehumidifier
  • Moving equipment to a new location
  • Repairing drywall or ceilings for access

Older homes with original attic ducts are a common case where duct work is worth doing at the same time, since a new system can't perform well through leaky, crushed ducts.

How do you compare installation quotes?

Lay the estimates side by side and check that each one spells out:

  • The exact equipment model numbers for every piece, including the coil
  • The system size and how it was determined
  • Whether refrigerant lines are new or reused
  • Permit, inspection and any required testing
  • Duct work, if any, and what it covers
  • Thermostat model
  • Haul-away of old equipment

A lower number that leaves out several of these isn't really cheaper. It may just move costs to a later change order.

What should happen at the end of the install?

Before the crew leaves, you should get a walkthrough of the new system, a demonstration of the thermostat, a note of the filter size and location, and paperwork showing the equipment model and serial numbers. Ask how the manufacturer's warranty gets registered, since some require registration within a set time.

faqs: How long does a new HVAC installation take?
Many straightforward replacements take one to two days. Jobs with duct replacement, a new equipment location or electrical upgrades can take longer. Your estimate should give you a time frame.
Do I need new ductwork with a new HVAC system?
Not always. If your ducts are in good shape, properly sized and sealed, they can be reused. Ducts that are crushed, leaking, undersized or very old often limit how well a new system performs.
Should the new system be the same size as my old one?
Not necessarily. The old system may have been sized wrong, or the home may have changed. A proper load calculation looks at the house itself rather than copying the old unit.
Does a new system come with a new thermostat?
Most installs include a new thermostat that's compatible with the equipment. Some systems work best with the manufacturer's own control, especially variable-speed models.
